modules.title: 01. Your developer setup
modules.description: Set up the tools you will use every day: a Linux shell, an editor, Python virtual environments and package managers. Everything later assumes this works.

lessons.title: Set up a Linux shell, an editor and a project folder
objectives: Install Ubuntu through WSL (on Windows) or open the Terminal (on macOS/Linux) and run basic commands.
Install VS Code with the Python and Remote/WSL extensions and open a folder from the terminal.
Explain what the terminal, the shell, the editor and the file system each do.

topics.title: Why Linux matters
details: Most servers, containers and cloud machines run Linux, so interviews and jobs assume you can use a Linux shell.
On Windows, WSL runs a real Ubuntu next to Windows; files live under \\wsl$ and your Linux home is /home/<you>.

topics.title: Terminal, shell and editor
details: The terminal is the window; the shell (bash or zsh) reads your commands; the editor (VS Code) edits files.
Run `code .` inside a folder to open it in VS Code connected to the same Linux environment.

topics.title: First commands
details: `pwd` (where am I), `ls -la` (what is here), `cd` (move), `mkdir -p` (make folders), `cat`/`less` (read files).
Tab completes names; the up arrow repeats commands; `man ls` or `ls --help` shows options.

video.locator: Watch the whole lecture; pause and type every command shown.

reading.locator: Install Linux on Windows with WSL: 'Install WSL command' and 'Set up your Linux username and password'. Skip if you are on macOS or Linux.

assignment.title: Make your workstation ready
instructions: Install WSL Ubuntu (Windows) or open Terminal (macOS/Linux). Run `uname -a` and note the output.
Install VS Code and the Python extension; on Windows also the WSL extension.
Create ~/code/playground, open it with `code .`, create hello.py printing your name, and run it with `python3 hello.py`.
Write a five-line note explaining terminal, shell, editor, file system and where your project folder is.
deliverables: Screenshot or transcript of `uname -a`, `pwd` and the program output.
Your five-line note.
acceptanceCriteria: hello.py runs from the terminal inside the Linux environment.
The note correctly separates terminal, shell and editor.

questions.prompt: What does `code .` do?
questions.answer: Opens the current folder in VS Code.
questions.explanation: The dot means 'this directory'.

questions.prompt: Why learn Linux if your laptop runs Windows?
questions.answer: Servers, containers and cloud machines mostly run Linux.
questions.explanation: Interview and job tasks assume a Linux shell.

reviewPrompts: Explain WSL to a friend in two sentences.
Which three commands do you use to find where you are and what is in a folder?

lessons.title: Isolate Python projects with virtual environments and package managers
objectives: Create and activate a Python virtual environment and install packages into it.
Pin dependencies in requirements.txt so another machine can reproduce your setup.
Use apt (system packages), pip (Python) and npm (JavaScript) for the right jobs.

topics.title: Why isolate
details: Different projects need different library versions; a virtual environment (.venv) keeps each project's packages separate.
Never install project packages with sudo pip into the system Python.

topics.title: The workflow
details: `python3 -m venv .venv` then `source .venv/bin/activate`; your prompt shows (.venv).
`pip install requests`, `pip freeze > requirements.txt`, and on a new machine `pip install -r requirements.txt`.

topics.title: Other package managers
details: `sudo apt install git curl build-essential` installs system tools on Ubuntu.
Node.js projects use npm with package.json and package-lock.json; the idea is the same: declared, pinned dependencies.

reading.locator: Installing Packages tutorial: sections 'Creating Virtual Environments', 'Use pip for Installing' and 'Requirements files'.

assignment.title: Reproduce an environment from scratch
instructions: In ~/code/playground create .venv, activate it and install `requests` and `pytest`.
Write fetch.py that downloads https://api.github.com and prints the HTTP status code.
Freeze to requirements.txt, delete .venv, recreate it from requirements.txt and run fetch.py again.
Add .venv to a .gitignore file and explain why it should not be committed.
deliverables: requirements.txt and .gitignore.
Terminal transcript of the recreate-and-run step.
acceptanceCriteria: fetch.py works after rebuilding the environment only from requirements.txt.
.venv is ignored.

questions.prompt: Why should .venv not be committed to Git?
questions.answer: It is machine-specific and large; requirements.txt recreates it.
questions.explanation: Commit the recipe, not the installed files.

questions.prompt: Which file pins exact Python package versions?
questions.answer: requirements.txt (from pip freeze).
questions.explanation: It lets others install the same versions.

reviewPrompts: What problem does a virtual environment solve?
When would you use apt instead of pip?

modules.title: 02. Linux and Bash for everyday engineering
modules.description: Work comfortably on a Linux machine: permissions, processes, logs, environment variables, remote access and small automation scripts.

lessons.title: Users, permissions and the file system layout
objectives: Read and change file permissions with ls -l, chmod and chown.
Explain users, groups, root and when sudo is appropriate.
Navigate the standard directories: /home, /etc, /var/log, /tmp, /usr/bin.

topics.title: Permission bits
details: `-rwxr-x---` means owner can read/write/execute, group can read/execute, others nothing.
`chmod 640 file` and `chmod u+x script.sh` change permissions; `chown user:group file` changes ownership.

topics.title: Root and sudo
details: root can do anything; `sudo` runs one command as root and is logged. Use it for system changes only.
Most permission errors are fixed by using the right user or folder, not by `chmod 777`.

topics.title: Where things live
details: Config in /etc, logs in /var/log, programs in /usr/bin, temporary files in /tmp, your files in /home/<you>.
`which python3` and `type ls` show which program a command runs.

reading.locator: The Linux Command Line, Part 1: chapters 'Exploring the System', 'Permissions' and 'Processes'.

assignment.title: Permission lab
instructions: Create a folder secrets-demo with a file note.txt. Make it readable only by you (chmod 600) and confirm with ls -l.
Write run.sh that prints the date; try running it before and after `chmod u+x run.sh`.
Find three config files in /etc and one log in /var/log; record what each is for.
Explain why `chmod 777` is a bad fix in three sentences.
deliverables: ls -l output before and after each change.
Short notes on the files you found.
acceptanceCriteria: note.txt shows -rw------- and run.sh runs only after adding execute permission.
The explanation names a concrete risk of 777.

questions.prompt: What does chmod 600 give?
questions.answer: Read and write for the owner only.
questions.explanation: 6 = read(4)+write(2); 0 = nothing for group and others.

questions.prompt: Where are system logs usually stored?
questions.answer: /var/log
questions.explanation: journalctl also reads systemd logs.

reviewPrompts: Decode the permission string -rwxr-x--x.
When is sudo the right tool?

lessons.title: Processes, environment variables, services and logs
objectives: Inspect running processes with ps, top/htop and stop one safely with kill.
Set and read environment variables and explain how programs inherit them.
Read service logs with journalctl and follow a log file with tail -f.

topics.title: Processes
details: Every running program is a process with a PID; `ps aux | grep python` finds it, `kill <PID>` asks it to stop.
Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the foreground program; `&` runs in the background; `jobs` and `fg` manage it.

topics.title: Environment variables
details: `export APP_ENV=dev` sets a variable for child processes; `echo $PATH` shows where commands are searched.
Secrets such as API keys are passed as environment variables or files, never hard-coded in code.

topics.title: Services and logs
details: systemd runs long-lived services: `systemctl status ssh`; logs via `journalctl -u ssh --since today`.
`tail -f app.log` follows a log live; `grep -i error app.log | wc -l` counts errors.

video.locator: Job control and environment variables sections.

reading.locator: The Linux Command Line: chapters 'Processes' and 'The Environment'.

assignment.title: Observe and control a program
instructions: Write loop.py that prints a counter every second and reads a GREETING environment variable.
Run it with `GREETING=hi python3 loop.py > out.log &`, find its PID with ps, follow the log with tail -f.
Stop it with kill and confirm it is gone.
Run `journalctl --since '10 min ago' | tail` (WSL may need systemd enabled) or explain why it is unavailable.
deliverables: Commands and outputs for each step.
loop.py.
acceptanceCriteria: The program reads GREETING from the environment.
Only the exercise process is stopped, by PID.

questions.prompt: How do you pass a secret to a program without hard-coding it?
questions.answer: Through an environment variable or a protected file.
questions.explanation: Code and Git history must not contain secrets.

questions.prompt: What does tail -f do?
questions.answer: Shows new lines of a file as they are written.
questions.explanation: Useful for watching logs live.

reviewPrompts: Explain PATH in one sentence.
How would you find which process is using the most CPU?

lessons.title: Pipes, text tools, SSH and small Bash scripts
objectives: Combine grep, sort, uniq, cut, awk and wc with pipes to answer questions about text data.
Connect to a remote machine with SSH keys and copy files with scp.
Write a Bash script with variables, arguments, conditions, loops and `set -euo pipefail`.

topics.title: Pipelines
details: `cat access.log | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head` lists top client IPs.
Redirect output with `>`, append with `>>`, send errors with `2>`; `| tee file` saves and shows.

topics.title: SSH
details: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` creates a key pair; the public key goes on the server, the private key never leaves your machine.
`ssh user@host`, `scp file user@host:/path`; GitHub also uses your SSH key.

topics.title: Scripting
details: Start scripts with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and `set -euo pipefail` so they stop on errors and unset variables.
`$1` is the first argument; `if [[ -f "$1" ]]; then ... fi`; `for f in *.csv; do ... done`; always quote variables.

video.locator: Watch fully and do the exercises at the end of the notes page.

reading.locator: GNU Bash Reference Manual: section 3.2.3 Pipelines, 3.6 Redirections and 6.4 Bash Conditional Expressions.

assignment.title: Log report script
instructions: Generate a fake access log of 1,000 lines with Python (random IPs, paths, status codes).
Write report.sh that takes the log path as an argument and prints: total requests, top 5 IPs, count of 5xx errors.
Make the script fail with a clear message if the file does not exist; use set -euo pipefail.
Create an SSH key and add it to your GitHub account; test with `ssh -T git@github.com`.
deliverables: report.sh and sample output.
Proof the GitHub SSH test succeeded (no private key shown).
acceptanceCriteria: report.sh output matches a Python-computed check on the same file.
Missing-file case exits non-zero with a message.

questions.prompt: What does `set -e` do in a script?
questions.answer: Stops the script when a command fails.
questions.explanation: Without it, errors are silently ignored.

questions.prompt: Which SSH key do you share?
questions.answer: Only the public key (.pub).
questions.explanation: The private key stays on your machine.

reviewPrompts: Write a one-line pipeline that counts unique words in a file.
Why quote "$var" in Bash?

modules.title: 03. Git and GitHub collaboration
modules.description: Go beyond commit and push: branches, merges, conflicts, pull requests, code review and automated checks with GitHub Actions. Every role uses this daily.

lessons.title: Branches, merges, rebases and conflicts
objectives: Create feature branches, merge them and explain fast-forward versus merge commits.
Resolve a merge conflict by hand and verify the result.
Undo safely with git restore, git revert and git reset --soft, and know when not to rewrite history.

topics.title: The model
details: A commit is a snapshot; a branch is a movable name pointing at a commit; HEAD is where you are.
`git switch -c feature/login`, `git merge feature/login`, `git log --oneline --graph --all`.

topics.title: Conflicts
details: A conflict happens when two branches change the same lines; Git marks them with <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>.
Edit the file to the correct final content, `git add` it, then continue the merge or rebase. Run the tests after.

topics.title: Rebase and undo
details: `git rebase main` replays your commits on top of main for a straight history; never rebase commits others already pulled.
`git revert <sha>` undoes a pushed commit with a new commit; `git restore file` discards local edits.

video.locator: Branching and merging part of the lecture.

reading.locator: Pro Git chapter 3 'Git Branching' (3.1-3.6) and section 2.4 'Undoing Things'.

assignment.title: Create and resolve a conflict
instructions: In a new repo, commit a file recipe.txt with five lines on main.
Create branch a and branch b; change line 3 differently on each and commit.
Merge a into main, then merge b and resolve the conflict to a sensible combined line.
Repeat using rebase instead of merge in a copy of the repo and compare `git log --graph`.
deliverables: Both graph outputs.
A short explanation of when you would choose merge or rebase.
acceptanceCriteria: The final file has no conflict markers and both histories are explained correctly.

questions.prompt: What is a branch in Git?
questions.answer: A movable pointer to a commit.
questions.explanation: Creating one is cheap; it is just a name.

questions.prompt: How do you undo a commit that is already pushed and shared?
questions.answer: git revert <commit>.
questions.explanation: Revert adds a new commit instead of rewriting shared history.

reviewPrompts: Draw the commit graph after a fast-forward merge.
Why is rebasing shared commits dangerous?

lessons.title: Pull requests, code review and a good README
objectives: Open a pull request from a branch, request review and respond to comments.
Write small, focused commits with clear messages.
Write a README that lets a stranger set up and run your project in five minutes.

topics.title: Pull request flow
details: Push a branch, open a PR describing what and why, link an issue, keep it small (under ~400 changed lines).
Reviewers comment on lines; you push fixes to the same branch; squash-merge keeps main tidy.

topics.title: Commit messages
details: Imperative summary under ~50 characters ('Add retry to payment client'), blank line, then the why.
One logical change per commit makes review and revert easy.

topics.title: README essentials
details: What it is, why it exists, setup commands, how to run tests, example output, architecture sketch, limitations.
Recruiters open your GitHub; a clear README is often the first evidence they read.

reading.locator: About pull requests, then the linked pages 'Creating a pull request' and 'Reviewing proposed changes in a pull request'.

assignment.title: Review loop on your own repo
instructions: Create a GitHub repository for your playground project and push main.
Make a feature branch that adds a function plus a test; open a pull request with a description template (What, Why, How tested).
Review your own PR line by line, leave two comments, address them in new commits, then squash-merge.
Write a README with setup, run, test and limitations sections.
deliverables: Link to the merged pull request.
The README.
acceptanceCriteria: The PR has a description, at least two review comments and follow-up commits.
A fresh clone can follow the README to run the tests.

questions.prompt: Why keep pull requests small?
questions.answer: They are easier to review well and safer to revert.
questions.explanation: Large PRs hide bugs.

questions.prompt: What should a README let a stranger do?
questions.answer: Set up, run and test the project quickly.
questions.explanation: It is the front door of a repository.

reviewPrompts: Rewrite a vague commit message 'fixed stuff' into a good one.
List the sections of your README template.

lessons.title: Automate checks with GitHub Actions
objectives: Explain workflows, jobs, steps, runners and triggers.
Write a workflow that installs dependencies and runs tests on every push and pull request.
Read a failing CI log and fix the cause.

topics.title: Concepts
details: A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows; it runs on events like push and pull_request.
Jobs run on runners (fresh virtual machines); steps either run shell commands or use actions like actions/checkout.

topics.title: A minimal Python workflow
details: Checkout, setup-python, `pip install -r requirements.txt`, `pytest -q`.
Add a status badge to the README; protect main so PRs must pass checks before merging.

topics.title: Secrets in CI
details: Store keys in repository Secrets and read them as `${{ secrets.NAME }}`; never echo them in logs.
Forked PRs do not receive secrets by default, which protects you.

reading.locator: GitHub Actions documentation: 'Understanding GitHub Actions' and the quickstart 'Building and testing Python'.

assignment.title: Add CI to your repo
instructions: Add .github/workflows/ci.yml running pytest on push and pull_request with Python 3.12.
Open a PR with a deliberately failing test; read the log and fix it.
Add a CI badge to the README and enable branch protection requiring the check.
deliverables: ci.yml and links to one failing and one passing run.
acceptanceCriteria: CI blocks merging while the test fails and passes after the fix.

questions.prompt: Where do GitHub Actions workflow files live?
questions.answer: .github/workflows/ in the repository.
questions.explanation: Each YAML file there is a workflow.

questions.prompt: How should CI read an API key?
questions.answer: From an encrypted repository secret.
questions.explanation: Never commit or print secrets.

reviewPrompts: Name the four building blocks of a workflow.
What does branch protection add to CI?

modules.title: 04. Data structures and algorithms for interviews
modules.description: Learn the problem patterns that product companies test, from arrays and hashing to graphs and dynamic programming, with a weekly practice routine.

lessons.title: Arrays, hashing, two pointers and sliding windows
objectives: State the time and space complexity of common array and hash map operations.
Recognise when a problem is solved by a hash map, two pointers or a sliding window.
Solve and explain eight classic problems in Python with tests.

topics.title: Complexity first
details: Big-O counts how work grows with input size n: O(1) lookup in a hash map, O(n) scan, O(n log n) sort, O(n^2) nested loops.
Always state time and space complexity out loud in interviews.

topics.title: Patterns
details: Hash map: count or remember seen values (Two Sum, Group Anagrams).
Two pointers: sorted array or palindrome checks moving inward. Sliding window: longest substring without repeats, max sum of k items.

topics.title: How to practise
details: Read, restate, give examples, brute force, optimise, code, test edge cases (empty, one item, duplicates, negatives).
If stuck for 25 minutes, read the solution, then re-solve it from memory two days later.

video.locator: Whole lecture: searching, sorting and running time.

reading.locator: Problem Solving with Algorithms and Data Structures: chapter 'Analysis' (Big-O notation and the performance of Python lists and dictionaries) and the 'Hashing' section of the 'Searching and Sorting' chapter.

assignment.title: Eight pattern problems
instructions: From the NeetCode roadmap 'Arrays & Hashing', 'Two Pointers' and 'Sliding Window' sections, solve 8 problems (at least 3 medium).
For each, write the brute force idea, the optimised idea, complexity and pytest cases.
Keep a log: date, problem, pattern, time taken, mistakes.
deliverables: Repository folder dsa/arrays with solutions, tests and the log.
acceptanceCriteria: Every solution passes its tests including edge cases.
Each entry states correct time and space complexity.

questions.prompt: Average time to look up a key in a hash map?
questions.explanation: Hash maps trade memory for constant-time lookup on average.

questions.prompt: When does a sliding window apply?
questions.answer: When the answer is a contiguous subarray or substring with a condition.
questions.explanation: You expand and shrink the window instead of rechecking everything.

reviewPrompts: Explain Two Sum's O(n) solution.
What edge cases do you test for array problems?

lessons.title: Stacks, queues, linked lists and binary search
objectives: Implement a stack, queue and singly linked list and know their operation costs.
Apply binary search to sorted arrays and to 'search the answer' problems.
Solve eight problems from these patterns with tests.

topics.title: Stacks and queues
details: Stack (LIFO) for matching brackets, undo, monotonic-stack 'next greater element'.
Queue (FIFO) with collections.deque for breadth-first processing.

topics.title: Linked lists
details: Reverse a list, detect a cycle with slow/fast pointers, merge two sorted lists; draw pointers on paper.
A dummy head node removes special cases at the start of the list.

topics.title: Binary search
details: Halve the search space each step: O(log n). Write the loop invariant: answer is always in [lo, hi].
Works on any monotonic condition, e.g. 'smallest capacity that ships packages in D days'.

video.locator: Whole lecture: linked lists, trees and hash tables.

reading.locator: Chapter 'Basic Data Structures' (stacks, queues, deques, linked lists) and 'The Binary Search' section of the 'Searching and Sorting' chapter.

assignment.title: Eight more pattern problems
instructions: Solve 8 problems from NeetCode 'Stack', 'Binary Search' and 'Linked List' (at least 3 medium).
Implement your own Stack and LinkedList classes with tests before using built-ins.
Add each to your practice log with pattern and mistakes.
deliverables: dsa/stack-search folder with solutions, tests and log updates.
acceptanceCriteria: Binary search solutions state their loop invariant in a comment.
All tests pass.

questions.prompt: Time complexity of binary search?
questions.answer: O(log n).
questions.explanation: Each step halves the remaining range.

questions.prompt: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list in O(1) space?
questions.answer: Slow and fast pointers (Floyd's algorithm).
questions.explanation: If they meet, there is a cycle.

reviewPrompts: When would you choose deque over list in Python?
State the binary search invariant you use.

lessons.title: Trees, graphs, heaps and BFS/DFS
objectives: Traverse binary trees recursively and iteratively (pre/in/post-order, level order).
Model problems as graphs and apply BFS for shortest steps and DFS for connectivity.
Use a heap (heapq) for top-k and scheduling problems.

topics.title: Trees
details: Binary search tree property: left < node < right; in-order traversal returns sorted values.
Most tree problems are 'solve for children, combine at the node' recursion: height, diameter, validate BST.

topics.title: Graphs
details: Store as adjacency lists (dict of lists). BFS with a queue finds the fewest steps in unweighted graphs; DFS with recursion or a stack explores components.
Grids are graphs: count islands with DFS; topological sort orders tasks with dependencies.

topics.title: Heaps
details: heapq gives O(log n) push/pop of the smallest item; keep a size-k heap for 'top k frequent'.
Dijkstra's shortest path uses a heap for weighted graphs.

reading.locator: Chapter 'Trees and Tree Algorithms' (traversals, binary heaps, binary search trees) and chapter 'Graphs and Graph Algorithms' (breadth-first search, depth-first search, topological sorting, Dijkstra).

assignment.title: Ten tree and graph problems
instructions: Solve 10 problems from NeetCode 'Trees', 'Heap / Priority Queue' and 'Graphs' (at least 5 medium).
For two graph problems, draw the graph and write the BFS/DFS order by hand before coding.
Record time per problem; repeat any problem that took over 40 minutes after three days.
deliverables: dsa/trees-graphs folder with solutions, tests, drawings and log.
acceptanceCriteria: Each solution includes complexity and passes tests.
Repeated problems show faster times in the log.

questions.prompt: Which traversal gives the fewest steps in an unweighted graph?
questions.answer: Breadth-first search (BFS).
questions.explanation: BFS explores level by level.

questions.prompt: How do you get the k largest items efficiently?
questions.answer: Keep a min-heap of size k.
questions.explanation: Push each item and pop when the heap exceeds k: O(n log k).

reviewPrompts: Explain recursion on trees using tree height as the example.
How would you detect a cycle in a dependency graph?

lessons.title: Recursion, backtracking, dynamic programming and a weekly interview routine
objectives: Write backtracking solutions for subsets, permutations and combination sums.
Turn a recursive solution into dynamic programming with memoisation and then a table.
Follow a sustainable weekly routine and run a timed mock interview.

topics.title: Backtracking
details: Choose, explore, un-choose: build a partial answer, recurse, then undo the choice.
Prune branches that cannot lead to a valid answer to save time.

topics.title: Dynamic programming
details: DP = recursion + remembering answers to overlapping subproblems (climbing stairs, coin change, longest common subsequence).
Define the state, the transition and the base case in words before coding; then use @functools.cache or a table.

topics.title: Interview routine
details: Aim for 5-7 problems a week mixed across patterns, one timed 45-minute mock, and revisiting failed problems.
Talk while you code: clarify, plan, code, test; interviewers grade communication as much as the answer.

reading.locator: Chapter 'Recursion', including its final section 'Dynamic Programming'.

assignment.title: DP set and a mock interview
instructions: Solve 8 problems from NeetCode 'Backtracking', '1-D Dynamic Programming' and '2-D Dynamic Programming'.
For two DP problems write the recursive, memoised and table versions and compare speed.
Do one 45-minute timed mock (with a friend or speaking aloud to a recording) on an unseen medium problem; write a short self-review.
deliverables: dsa/dp folder, the timing comparison and the mock self-review.
acceptanceCriteria: Each DP solution names its state, transition and base case.
The self-review lists two concrete improvements.

questions.prompt: What makes a problem suitable for DP?
questions.answer: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.
questions.explanation: The same subproblem is solved many times.

questions.prompt: What are the three steps of backtracking?
questions.answer: Choose, explore (recurse), un-choose.
questions.explanation: Undoing the choice lets you try the next option.

reviewPrompts: Explain coin change's DP state.
What is your weekly practice plan?

modules.title: 05. Object-oriented design and clean code
modules.description: Write code that others can read, test and change: classes and interfaces, type hints, small functions, naming and refactoring.

lessons.title: Classes, interfaces and composition
objectives: Model a small domain with classes, dataclasses and abstract base classes in Python.
Prefer composition over inheritance and explain the trade-off.
Apply encapsulation and the single-responsibility principle.

topics.title: Objects
details: A class bundles data and behaviour; `@dataclass` removes boilerplate for data holders.
Encapsulation: hide internal details behind methods so callers cannot break invariants (e.g. balance never negative).

topics.title: Interfaces
details: An interface (abc.ABC or typing.Protocol) says what an object can do, not how. Code depends on the interface so implementations can be swapped (e.g. FakeEmailSender in tests).

topics.title: Design principles
details: Single responsibility: one reason to change per class. Composition: a Car has an Engine rather than inheriting from it.
These ideas transfer directly to Java, Go and TypeScript used in later modules.

reading.locator: Python Tutorial chapter 9 'Classes' and the library reference for dataclasses and abc.

assignment.title: Library system model
instructions: Model a small library: Book, Member, Loan with rules (max 3 loans, no double loan of a copy).
Define a Notifier protocol with EmailNotifier and FakeNotifier; Library depends only on the protocol.
Write pytest tests using FakeNotifier for the borrowing rules.
deliverables: Code and tests.
A class diagram sketch.
acceptanceCriteria: Rules are enforced inside the classes, not by callers.
Tests run without any real email.

questions.prompt: Why depend on an interface instead of a concrete class?
questions.answer: So implementations can be swapped, for example a fake in tests.
questions.explanation: This keeps code testable and flexible.

questions.prompt: Composition or inheritance for 'a Car has an Engine'?
questions.answer: Composition.
questions.explanation: Has-a relationships are composition; is-a may be inheritance.

reviewPrompts: Explain encapsulation with your Loan rule.
When is inheritance appropriate?

lessons.title: Readable code, type hints and refactoring
objectives: Spot common code smells: long functions, duplicated code, unclear names, deep nesting.
Refactor safely in small steps with tests as a safety net.
Add type hints and run a type checker and linter (mypy, ruff).

topics.title: Smells and fixes
details: Long function -> extract function; duplicate logic -> one helper; magic numbers -> named constants; nested ifs -> early returns.
Names should say what, not how: `unpaid_invoices` beats `list2`.

topics.title: Safe refactoring
details: Tests first, then one small change at a time, running tests after each; commit often.
Refactoring changes structure, never behaviour.

topics.title: Tooling
details: Type hints (`def total(items: list[Item]) -> Decimal`) document intent and catch bugs with mypy.
ruff formats and lints; add both to CI so style never becomes a review argument.

reading.locator: Refactoring.Guru: 'What is Refactoring', 'Code Smells' (Bloaters and Dispensables) and the 'Composing Methods' refactorings.

assignment.title: Refactor a messy script
instructions: Take a 100+ line script you wrote earlier (or write a deliberately messy one) and add tests that pin its behaviour.
Refactor in at least six small commits: extract functions, rename, remove duplication, add type hints.
Add ruff and mypy to CI and fix all findings.
deliverables: Before/after code and the commit list.
CI run passing with ruff and mypy.
acceptanceCriteria: Tests pass after every commit.
mypy reports no errors.

questions.prompt: What must not change during a refactor?
questions.answer: The program's behaviour.
questions.explanation: Only the structure changes; tests prove it.

questions.prompt: Fix for deeply nested if statements?
questions.answer: Use early returns (guard clauses).
questions.explanation: It flattens the code and clarifies the main path.

reviewPrompts: List three smells you found in your code.
Why add linting to CI?

modules.title: 06. SQL beyond the basics
modules.description: Write the SQL that interviews and real jobs need: joins, grouping, window functions and CTEs, then understand indexes, transactions and query plans.

lessons.title: Joins, aggregation, CTEs and window functions
objectives: Choose INNER, LEFT and anti-joins correctly and predict row counts.
Use GROUP BY with HAVING and CTEs to break a question into steps.
Use window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, running SUM) for ranking and time comparisons.

topics.title: Joins
details: INNER keeps matches only; LEFT keeps all left rows with NULLs when unmatched; `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL` finds missing matches.
Duplicate keys multiply rows; always check row counts before and after a join.

topics.title: Grouping and CTEs
details: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after.
`WITH monthly AS (...) SELECT ... FROM monthly` keeps complex queries readable.

topics.title: Window functions
details: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY ordered_at DESC)` picks each customer's latest order.
`LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month)` compares with the previous month; `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY day)` gives running totals.

video.locator: Whole lecture on joins and relationships.

reading.locator: PostgreSQL manual: Tutorial section 2.6 'Joins Between Tables', 2.7 'Aggregate Functions' and 3.5 'Window Functions'; reference 7.8 'WITH Queries'.

assignment.title: Twenty analytics questions
instructions: Load a small sample database (create tables customers, orders, order_items, products with 200+ generated rows) in PostgreSQL or SQLite.
Answer 20 questions including: top 3 products per category, month-over-month revenue change, customers with no orders, running total per day.
For five queries, compute the answer independently in Python and compare.
deliverables: SQL file with the 20 queries and results.
The Python cross-checks.
acceptanceCriteria: Cross-checked answers match exactly.
At least five queries use window functions.

questions.prompt: How do you find customers with no orders?
questions.answer: LEFT JOIN orders and keep rows where the order id IS NULL.
questions.explanation: This is an anti-join.

questions.prompt: Difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
questions.explanation: Aggregates are not available in WHERE.

reviewPrompts: Write a query for each customer's second order.
Why can a join increase row counts?

lessons.title: Indexes, transactions, isolation and query plans
objectives: Explain how a B-tree index speeds up lookups and what it costs on writes.
Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE output and tell a sequential scan from an index scan.
Explain ACID, transactions and the common isolation anomalies.

topics.title: Indexes
details: An index is a sorted structure pointing to rows; it turns O(n) scans into O(log n) lookups for selective filters.
Indexes slow inserts/updates and use disk; index columns you filter, join or sort on.

topics.title: Query plans
details: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...` shows the plan with real timings; look for Seq Scan on large tables and row-estimate mismatches.

topics.title: Transactions
details: ACID: atomic (all or nothing), consistent, isolated, durable. `BEGIN; ... COMMIT;` or ROLLBACK.
Isolation levels trade safety for concurrency: lost updates and write skew are prevented by SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or SERIALIZABLE.

reading.locator: PostgreSQL manual: chapter 11 'Indexes' (11.1-11.3), section 14.1 'Using EXPLAIN' and chapter 13 'Concurrency Control' (13.1-13.2).

assignment.title: Measure an index and a race
instructions: Create a table with 1,000,000 generated rows; time a filtered query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after adding an index.
Open two psql sessions and reproduce a lost update on an account balance, then prevent it with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
Write a one-page note with both plans and the explanation.
deliverables: Both EXPLAIN outputs, timings and the session transcripts.
acceptanceCriteria: The plan changes from Seq Scan to Index Scan with a measured speed-up.
The lost update is reproduced and then prevented.

questions.prompt: What is the cost of adding an index?
questions.answer: Slower writes and extra storage.
questions.explanation: Every insert or update must also update the index.

questions.prompt: What does SELECT ... FOR UPDATE do?
questions.answer: Locks the selected rows until the transaction ends.
questions.explanation: Other writers wait, preventing lost updates.

reviewPrompts: Explain ACID with a bank transfer.
How do you decide which column to index?

modules.title: 07. Networks and the web
modules.description: Understand what happens between your code and another machine: IP, TCP, DNS, TLS, HTTP, REST APIs and JSON.

lessons.title: IP, ports, TCP, DNS and TLS
objectives: Explain IP addresses, ports, TCP versus UDP and the TCP handshake.
Trace a DNS lookup with dig and explain record types (A, CNAME, MX).
Explain what TLS provides and inspect a certificate.

topics.title: Addresses and ports
details: An IP address finds a machine; a port finds a program on it (HTTPS 443, PostgreSQL 5432, SSH 22).
TCP gives reliable ordered delivery with a 3-way handshake; UDP is faster but unreliable (DNS, video).

topics.title: DNS
details: DNS turns names into IPs: `dig example.com A`; CNAME aliases another name; TTL controls caching.
Many 'the site is down' incidents are DNS or certificate problems.

topics.title: TLS
details: TLS encrypts traffic and proves the server's identity with a certificate signed by a trusted authority.
`openssl s_client -connect github.com:443` or the browser lock icon shows the certificate chain and expiry.

reading.locator: MDN: 'An overview of HTTP' and 'Evolution of HTTP', plus the glossary entries for TCP, DNS and TLS linked from those pages.

assignment.title: Trace a request
instructions: Use dig to resolve three domains; record A/CNAME records and TTLs.
Use `curl -v https://example.com` and label the DNS, TCP connect, TLS handshake and HTTP request parts of the output.
Inspect a certificate's issuer and expiry with openssl.
Write a 10-step explanation of what happens when you type a URL and press Enter.
deliverables: Annotated outputs and the 10-step explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: The explanation covers DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP request/response and rendering in the right order.

questions.prompt: Default port for HTTPS?
questions.explanation: HTTP uses 80.

questions.prompt: What two things does TLS provide?
questions.answer: Encryption and server authentication (and integrity).
questions.explanation: The certificate proves who you are talking to.

reviewPrompts: What happens when you type a URL? (Practise this classic interview question.)
TCP or UDP for a payment API, and why?

lessons.title: HTTP, REST APIs, JSON and authentication headers
objectives: Use HTTP methods and status codes correctly in API design.
Call a REST API with curl and Python, handling errors, timeouts and pagination.
Explain API keys, bearer tokens and cookies at a high level.

topics.title: HTTP semantics
details: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates, DELETE removes. GET must not change data.
2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (400 bad input, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 missing, 429 rate limited), 5xx server error.

topics.title: REST design
details: Resources are nouns: `/orders/42/items`; filters as query parameters; JSON bodies; consistent error format.
Idempotent methods (GET, PUT, DELETE) can be retried safely; POST needs an idempotency key to be safe to retry.

topics.title: Calling APIs
details: Python requests: set `timeout=`, check `response.raise_for_status()`, follow pagination links, back off on 429.
Auth: `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header; never put secrets in URLs.

video.locator: The HTTP portion of the lecture.

reading.locator: MDN: 'HTTP request methods', 'HTTP response status codes' and 'HTTP headers: Authorization'.

assignment.title: Robust API client
instructions: Write a Python client for the public GitHub REST API that lists a user's repositories across all pages.
Handle timeouts, non-200 responses and rate limiting (respect the reset header) with clear messages.
Write tests using a fake HTTP layer (responses or a mocked session) for success, 404 and 429.
deliverables: Client code and tests.
acceptanceCriteria: All pages are collected.
Tests cover success, not found and rate limiting without network calls.

questions.prompt: Difference between 401 and 403?
questions.answer: 401: not authenticated; 403: authenticated but not allowed.
questions.explanation: Identity versus permission.

questions.prompt: Why must GET not change data?
questions.answer: Clients, caches and crawlers may repeat GET requests freely.
questions.explanation: GET is defined as safe.

reviewPrompts: Design endpoints for a to-do app.
How would you retry a failed POST safely?

modules.title: 08. Docker and containers
modules.description: Package any app with its dependencies so it runs the same everywhere. Containers are required for every backend, data, ML and cloud role.

lessons.title: Images, containers, volumes and networking
objectives: Explain images versus containers and how layers are cached.
Run, inspect, stop and remove containers; map ports and mount volumes.
Run PostgreSQL in a container and connect from your machine.

topics.title: Concepts
details: An image is a read-only template (like a class); a container is a running instance (like an object).
Containers share the host kernel; they are lighter than virtual machines but are not a strong security boundary by default.

topics.title: Everyday commands
details: `docker run -d -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev postgres:17`, `docker ps`, `docker logs -f <id>`, `docker exec -it <id> bash`, `docker rm -f <id>`.
Port mapping host:container; `-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data` keeps data after the container is removed.

topics.title: Networks
details: Containers on the same user-defined network reach each other by container name (e.g. `db:5432`).

reading.locator: Docker Get started: 'What is a container?', 'What is an image?', 'Publishing and exposing ports' and 'Persisting container data'.

assignment.title: Database in a container
instructions: Install Docker (Docker Desktop with WSL integration, or Docker Engine on Linux).
Run PostgreSQL with a named volume; create a table and insert rows with psql.
Remove and recreate the container with the same volume and show the data survived.
Explain image, container, volume and port mapping in your own words.
deliverables: Command transcript and explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: Data persists across container recreation.
You can connect from the host on the mapped port.

questions.prompt: Image versus container?
questions.answer: An image is a template; a container is a running instance of it.
questions.explanation: Many containers can run from one image.

questions.prompt: How do you keep database data when the container is deleted?
questions.answer: Mount a volume.
questions.explanation: Volumes live outside the container's writable layer.

reviewPrompts: Why are containers lighter than VMs?
What does -p 8080:80 mean?

lessons.title: Dockerfiles and Docker Compose for multi-service apps
objectives: Write a Dockerfile for a Python web app with small, cache-friendly layers.
Use multi-stage builds and a non-root user.
Run an app plus database plus cache together with Docker Compose.

topics.title: Dockerfile
details: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY requirements first, RUN pip install, COPY code, USER app, EXPOSE, CMD.
Copying requirements before code means dependency layers are reused when only code changes.

topics.title: Smaller and safer images
details: Multi-stage builds compile in one stage and copy only results into a slim runtime image.
Run as a non-root user, add a .dockerignore, and never bake secrets into images.

topics.title: Compose
details: compose.yaml declares services (web, db, redis), ports, environment, volumes and depends_on with healthchecks.
`docker compose up --build`, `docker compose logs -f web`, `docker compose down -v`.

reading.locator: Docker Compose: 'How Compose works', 'Quickstart' and 'Control startup order'.

assignment.title: Containerise a small API
instructions: Write a FastAPI or Flask app with an endpoint that reads and writes PostgreSQL and caches a value in Redis.
Write a multi-stage Dockerfile running as a non-root user, plus .dockerignore.
Write compose.yaml for web, db and redis with healthchecks; run end to end.
Report the image size before and after the multi-stage build.
deliverables: Dockerfile, compose.yaml, app code and size comparison.
acceptanceCriteria: `docker compose up` starts all services and the endpoint works.
The container runs as a non-root user.

questions.prompt: Why COPY requirements.txt before the rest of the code?
questions.answer: So the dependency install layer is cached when only code changes.
questions.explanation: Builds become much faster.

questions.prompt: Why avoid putting secrets in a Dockerfile?
questions.answer: They are stored in image layers that anyone with the image can read.
questions.explanation: Pass secrets at runtime instead.

reviewPrompts: Explain multi-stage builds.
What does depends_on with a healthcheck guarantee?

modules.title: 09. Cloud fundamentals
modules.description: Learn what the cloud is, how accounts, regions and IAM work, the core services on AWS and Azure, and how to avoid surprise bills.

lessons.title: Cloud concepts, accounts, regions, IAM and billing safety
objectives: Explain IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, regions, availability zones and the shared responsibility model.
Create a cloud account safely: MFA on root, an admin user/role, a budget alert.
Read and write a basic IAM policy using least privilege.

topics.title: Concepts
details: IaaS (virtual machines), PaaS (managed databases, app services), SaaS (finished apps). You manage less as you go up.
A region is a geographic area; availability zones are separate data centres in it, used for high availability.

topics.title: Account safety
details: Turn on MFA for the root/owner account and stop using it day to day; use an IAM user or SSO role.
Create a monthly budget with email alerts before launching anything; delete resources after each practice session.

topics.title: IAM
details: A policy says which actions on which resources are allowed. Start with nothing and add only what is needed (least privilege).
Roles give temporary credentials to services and people; prefer them over long-lived access keys.

reading.locator: Overview of AWS: 'What is cloud computing?', 'Six advantages of cloud computing', 'Global infrastructure' and 'Security and compliance'.

assignment.title: Safe cloud account
instructions: Create an AWS free-tier account (or use Azure, since you hold AZ-900). Enable MFA on the root/owner.
Create a non-root admin identity and a budget of a small amount with an email alert.
Write an IAM policy that allows only reading one S3 bucket; test that it cannot delete objects.
Write down your teardown checklist.
deliverables: Screenshots with account IDs hidden, the policy JSON and the checklist.
acceptanceCriteria: MFA and a budget alert are on.
The policy allows read and denies delete in a test.

questions.prompt: What is the shared responsibility model?
questions.answer: The provider secures the cloud infrastructure; you secure what you put in it (data, identities, configuration).
questions.explanation: Most breaches are customer misconfiguration.

questions.prompt: First thing to do in a new cloud account?
questions.answer: Enable MFA on the root account and set a budget alert.
questions.explanation: Prevents takeover and surprise bills.

reviewPrompts: Explain region versus availability zone.
Why prefer roles over access keys?

lessons.title: Core services: compute, storage, databases, networking and serverless
objectives: Match common needs to services on AWS and Azure (VMs, object storage, managed databases, serverless functions).
Launch and connect to a small virtual machine and host a file in object storage.
Deploy a serverless function behind an HTTP endpoint and delete everything afterwards.

topics.title: Service map
details: Compute: EC2 / Azure Virtual Machines; containers: ECS/EKS / AKS; functions: Lambda / Azure Functions.
Storage: S3 / Blob Storage; databases: RDS / Azure SQL; NoSQL: DynamoDB / Cosmos DB (you are DP-420 certified).

topics.title: Networking
details: A VPC/VNet is your private network; subnets can be public or private; security groups/NSGs are firewalls on instances.
Never open SSH (22) to 0.0.0.0/0 for long; restrict to your IP.

topics.title: Serverless
details: Functions run on demand and you pay per call; great for small APIs and event handlers, with cold starts and time limits.

reading.locator: Overview of AWS: sections 'Compute services', 'Storage services', 'Database services', 'Networking and content delivery'.

assignment.title: Three-service tour
instructions: Launch the smallest free-tier VM, SSH in with a key, install nginx, view the page, then terminate it.
Create a private S3 bucket (or Blob container), upload a file and generate a time-limited pre-signed URL.
Deploy a 'hello' function behind an HTTP URL; call it with curl.
Confirm in the console that all resources are deleted and record the cost so far.
deliverables: Commands/screenshots, the service map table you made, final cost.
acceptanceCriteria: Every resource is deleted at the end.
The bucket is not public; access works only with the pre-signed URL.

questions.prompt: AWS equivalent of Azure Blob Storage?
questions.answer: Amazon S3.
questions.explanation: Both are object storage.

questions.prompt: Why put a database in a private subnet?
questions.answer: So it is not reachable from the internet, only from your app.
questions.explanation: Reduces attack surface.

reviewPrompts: Pick services for a photo-sharing app.
What are serverless trade-offs?

modules.title: 10. Math foundations for ML, data and quant
modules.description: The linear algebra, calculus and probability behind machine learning, statistics and quantitative finance, taught with code.

lessons.title: Linear algebra: vectors, matrices and what they do
objectives: Compute dot products, matrix products and norms by hand and with NumPy.
Interpret a matrix as a transformation and explain rank and inverses.
Explain eigenvectors and why they matter for PCA and risk models.

topics.title: Vectors
details: A vector is a list of numbers (a point or a direction). The dot product measures alignment; cosine similarity powers embeddings search.

topics.title: Matrices
details: A matrix transforms vectors; multiplying matrices composes transformations. Shapes must match: (m x n)(n x p).
A neural network layer is a matrix multiply plus a bias and a non-linearity.

topics.title: Eigen and decomposition
details: Eigenvectors keep their direction under a transformation; PCA uses the covariance matrix's eigenvectors to find main directions of variation.

reading.locator: Mathematics for Machine Learning chapter 2 'Linear Algebra' (2.1-2.6) and chapter 4 sections 4.2 and 4.4 on eigenvalues and eigendecomposition.

assignment.title: Linear algebra with NumPy
instructions: Implement dot product and matrix multiply with loops, compare against NumPy on random inputs.
Apply 2x2 rotation and scaling matrices to points and plot before/after.
Run PCA by hand on a 2-D dataset (covariance, eigenvectors) and compare with scikit-learn.
deliverables: Notebook with code, plots and explanations.
acceptanceCriteria: Your loop results match NumPy within floating-point tolerance.
Hand PCA directions match scikit-learn up to sign.

questions.prompt: What does cosine similarity measure?
questions.answer: The angle between two vectors (how aligned they are).
questions.explanation: Used to compare embeddings.

questions.prompt: Shape of (3x2) times (2x4)?
questions.explanation: Inner dimensions must match and disappear.

reviewPrompts: Explain a neural network layer in matrix terms.
Why does PCA use eigenvectors?

lessons.title: Calculus and gradients for optimisation
objectives: Compute derivatives and partial derivatives of simple functions.
Apply the chain rule and explain backpropagation at a high level.
Implement gradient descent for linear regression.

topics.title: Derivatives
details: A derivative is the slope: how fast output changes with input. The gradient collects partial derivatives for many inputs.

topics.title: Chain rule
details: For f(g(x)), the derivative is f'(g(x)) * g'(x). Backpropagation applies this from the loss back through each layer.

topics.title: Gradient descent
details: Repeat: compute the gradient of the loss, step against it by a learning rate. Too large diverges, too small is slow.
Option Greeks in quant (delta, gamma) are derivatives of price too.

reading.locator: Mathematics for Machine Learning chapter 5 'Vector Calculus' (5.1-5.3 and 5.6 on backpropagation) and section 7.1 'Optimization Using Gradient Descent'.

assignment.title: Gradient descent from scratch
instructions: Generate noisy data y = 3x + 2; fit w and b by gradient descent on mean squared error.
Plot the loss per step for three learning rates; explain what you see.
Check your gradient numerically with finite differences.
deliverables: Notebook with code, plots and explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: Fitted w and b are close to 3 and 2.
Analytic and numeric gradients agree.

questions.prompt: What does the gradient point toward?
questions.answer: The direction of steepest increase.
questions.explanation: Gradient descent steps the opposite way.

questions.prompt: What happens with too high a learning rate?
questions.answer: The loss oscillates or diverges.
questions.explanation: Steps overshoot the minimum.

reviewPrompts: Explain the chain rule with a two-layer example.
How would you check a gradient implementation?

lessons.title: Probability, distributions and expectation
objectives: Compute probabilities with conditional probability and Bayes' rule.
Describe Bernoulli, binomial, normal and Poisson distributions and simulate them.
Compute expectation and variance and explain the law of large numbers and central limit theorem.

topics.title: Rules
details: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B|A); Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B). Classic: a positive test for a rare disease is often a false positive.

topics.title: Distributions
details: Bernoulli/binomial for yes/no counts, Poisson for event counts per interval, normal for sums of many small effects.
Financial returns have fatter tails than a normal distribution; models that assume normality underestimate crashes.

topics.title: Expectation and limits
details: E[X] is the long-run average; variance measures spread. Sample means converge to E[X] (law of large numbers) and are roughly normal (CLT).

video.locator: Whole video; then continue to Part 2 on the same site.

reading.locator: probabilitycourse.com chapters 1 (basic concepts), 3 (discrete random variables) and 4 (continuous and normal distributions).

assignment.title: Simulate to understand
instructions: Solve the rare-disease Bayes problem analytically and by simulating 1,000,000 people.
Simulate dice sums for 1, 2, 10 and 30 dice and plot how the distribution approaches normal.
Estimate the expected number of coin flips to see two heads in a row by simulation and verify it analytically (answer: 6).
deliverables: Notebook with simulations, plots and analytic answers.
acceptanceCriteria: Simulated and analytic answers agree within sampling error.
Plots show the CLT effect.

questions.prompt: What does the central limit theorem say?
questions.answer: Averages of many independent samples are approximately normally distributed.
questions.explanation: Regardless of the original distribution (with finite variance).

questions.prompt: Expected value of a fair six-sided die?

reviewPrompts: Explain Bayes' rule with your own example.
Why are fat tails important in finance?

modules.title: 11. Operating systems and concurrency basics
modules.description: How programs actually run: processes, threads, memory and scheduling, and the bugs that appear when things run at the same time.

lessons.title: Processes, threads, memory and scheduling
objectives: Explain processes versus threads and what each shares.
Describe stack versus heap memory and virtual memory at a high level.
Explain CPU-bound versus I/O-bound work and why it decides your concurrency tool.

topics.title: Processes and threads
details: A process has its own memory; threads inside it share memory, which is fast but needs coordination.
Context switches cost time; too many threads can be slower than a few.

topics.title: Memory
details: The stack holds function calls and local variables; the heap holds objects that outlive a call.
Each process sees virtual addresses mapped to physical memory by the OS; running out leads to swapping or the OOM killer.

topics.title: Workload types
details: CPU-bound (number crunching) benefits from multiple cores/processes; I/O-bound (network, disk) benefits from async or threads.
In Python the GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so CPU work uses multiprocessing.

reading.locator: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces: chapters 4 'The Process', 13 'Address Spaces' and 26 'Concurrency: An Introduction'.

assignment.title: Measure CPU versus I/O work
instructions: Write a CPU-bound task (e.g. count primes) and an I/O-bound task (e.g. 50 HTTP requests to httpbin or sleep-based fakes).
Time each with sequential, threads (ThreadPoolExecutor) and processes (ProcessPoolExecutor).
Explain the results using the GIL and CPU/I/O-bound reasoning.
deliverables: Code, timing table and explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: Processes speed up CPU-bound work and threads speed up I/O-bound work in your measurements, or you explain why not.

questions.prompt: What do threads in one process share?
questions.answer: Memory (heap and globals) and open files.
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own stack.

questions.prompt: Python tool for CPU-bound parallelism?
questions.answer: multiprocessing / ProcessPoolExecutor.
questions.explanation: Separate processes avoid the GIL.

reviewPrompts: Process vs thread in one sentence each.
Stack vs heap?

lessons.title: Race conditions, locks, deadlocks and async programming
objectives: Reproduce a race condition and fix it with a lock.
Explain deadlock and two ways to prevent it.
Write async code with asyncio and explain the event loop.

topics.title: Races
details: A race condition happens when the result depends on timing, e.g. two threads doing `count += 1` lose updates.
Protect shared state with a lock, or avoid sharing by passing messages through queues.

topics.title: Deadlocks
details: Two threads each hold a lock the other needs and wait forever. Prevent by always acquiring locks in the same order or using timeouts.

topics.title: Async
details: asyncio runs many I/O tasks on one thread; `await` gives control back to the event loop while waiting.
Blocking calls (time.sleep, requests) inside async code freeze everything; use asyncio.sleep and async HTTP clients.

reading.locator: OSTEP chapters 28 'Locks' and 32 'Common Concurrency Problems' (deadlock section).

assignment.title: Break it, then fix it
instructions: Write a counter incremented 1,000,000 times by 4 threads without a lock; show lost updates (use a small sleep or bytecode-heavy loop if needed).
Fix it with threading.Lock and show the correct total.
Create a deadlock with two locks, then fix it by lock ordering.
Fetch 100 URLs (or fake delays) with asyncio and compare time to sequential.
deliverables: Code and outputs for all four parts with explanations.
acceptanceCriteria: Lost updates are shown and then fixed.
The async version is measurably faster for I/O.

questions.prompt: What is a race condition?
questions.answer: A bug where the result depends on the timing of concurrent operations.
questions.explanation: Shared mutable state without coordination causes it.

questions.prompt: How do you prevent a lock-ordering deadlock?
questions.answer: Always acquire multiple locks in the same global order.
questions.explanation: Circular wait becomes impossible.

reviewPrompts: Explain the event loop.
Locks versus message passing?

modules.title: 12. System design basics
modules.description: The building blocks behind every scalable system and the trade-offs between them. Needed for SDE, backend, data and cloud interviews.

lessons.title: Building blocks: load balancers, caches, queues, databases and CDNs
objectives: Explain what each building block does and when to add it.
Estimate traffic and storage with back-of-the-envelope numbers.
Draw an architecture for a simple app and justify each part.

topics.title: Blocks
details: Load balancer spreads requests over servers; cache (Redis) stores hot reads; queue (Kafka, SQS) decouples slow work; CDN serves static files near users.
Stateless app servers scale horizontally; state lives in databases and caches.

topics.title: Estimates
details: 1 million requests/day is about 12 per second on average; plan for peaks 5-10x higher.
Know rough latencies: memory ~100 ns, SSD read ~100 us, same-region network round trip ~0.5 ms, cross-continent ~150 ms.

topics.title: Approach
details: Clarify requirements, estimate, sketch the high level, deep-dive one component, discuss bottlenecks and failures.

reading.locator: System Design Primer: 'How to approach a system design interview question', 'Performance vs scalability', 'Latency vs throughput', and the sections on load balancers, caching and asynchronism.

assignment.title: Design a URL shortener
instructions: Write requirements (functional and non-functional) and estimates for 100M new URLs per month.
Draw the architecture with API, ID generation, database choice, cache and analytics queue.
Write how the design handles a 10x traffic spike and a cache failure.
deliverables: Design document (2-3 pages) with diagram.
acceptanceCriteria: Estimates are shown with arithmetic.
Each component is justified with a trade-off.

questions.prompt: Why make app servers stateless?
questions.answer: So any server can handle any request and you can add servers freely.
questions.explanation: State goes to shared stores.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many requests per second is 1M per day?
questions.answer: About 12 per second on average.

reviewPrompts: When do you add a queue?
Name four latency numbers.

lessons.title: Scaling data: replication, sharding, consistency and CAP
objectives: Explain leader-follower replication and replication lag.
Explain sharding strategies and the hot-key problem.
Explain CAP and strong versus eventual consistency with examples.

topics.title: Replication
details: Writes go to the leader; followers copy them for reads and failover. Reading from a follower may return stale data.

topics.title: Sharding
details: Split data across machines by key range or hash; choose a key that spreads load. A celebrity user can become a hot key.

topics.title: Consistency
details: During a network partition a system must choose consistency (refuse some requests) or availability (serve possibly stale data): CAP.
Bank balances want strong consistency; like counts can be eventually consistent.

reading.locator: System Design Primer: 'CAP theorem', 'Consistency patterns', 'Availability patterns' and 'Database' (replication, federation, sharding, denormalization).

assignment.title: Choose consistency per feature
instructions: For a social app, list six features (feed, likes, payments, follows, messages, notifications) and choose strong or eventual consistency for each with a reason.
Design sharding for the messages table and describe how you would avoid hot keys.
Explain what users see during replication lag and one mitigation (read-your-writes).
deliverables: Two-page write-up.
acceptanceCriteria: Each choice has a concrete reason tied to user impact.

questions.prompt: What is replication lag?
questions.answer: Delay before a write on the leader appears on followers.
questions.explanation: Reads from followers can be stale.

questions.prompt: Strong or eventual consistency for account balances?
questions.answer: Strong.
questions.explanation: Money must not be double-spent.

reviewPrompts: Explain CAP with an example.
Hash versus range sharding?

modules.title: 13. Security basics for every engineer
modules.description: The common ways software gets attacked and the basic habits that prevent it: input validation, authentication, secrets and encryption.

lessons.title: The OWASP Top 10, authentication and authorisation
objectives: Explain injection, broken access control, XSS and other OWASP Top 10 risks with examples.
Separate authentication (who you are) from authorisation (what you may do).
Prevent SQL injection with parameterised queries and verify with a test.

topics.title: Top risks
details: Broken access control: user A can read user B's order by changing an ID. Fix by checking ownership on every request.
Injection: building SQL with string formatting lets input become code. Use parameters (`cursor.execute('... WHERE id = %s', (id,))`).
XSS: unescaped user input in HTML runs scripts in other users' browsers; templates escape by default.

topics.title: Identity
details: Passwords are hashed with slow algorithms (bcrypt, argon2), never stored plain. MFA blocks most account takeovers.
Authorisation must be enforced on the server; hiding a button is not security.

reading.locator: OWASP Top 10: read the summary of each category, then A01 Broken Access Control and A03 Injection in full.

assignment.title: Find and fix two bugs
instructions: Write a tiny Flask/FastAPI app with an orders endpoint vulnerable to SQL injection and to reading other users' orders.
Exploit both locally with curl and record the payloads.
Fix both (parameterised query, ownership check) and add tests that the exploits now fail.
deliverables: Vulnerable and fixed code, exploit transcripts and tests.
acceptanceCriteria: Both exploits work before and fail after the fix.
Tests cover both cases.

questions.prompt: How do you prevent SQL injection?
questions.answer: Use parameterised queries.
questions.explanation: Input is sent as data, never as SQL code.

questions.prompt: Authentication vs authorisation?
questions.answer: Authentication proves who you are; authorisation decides what you may do.
questions.explanation: Both are needed on every request.

reviewPrompts: Explain broken access control with an example.
Why hash passwords slowly?

lessons.title: Secrets, hashing and encryption basics
objectives: Keep secrets out of code, logs and Git, and rotate one that leaked.
Distinguish hashing, encryption and encoding.
Use symmetric encryption from a trusted library correctly.

topics.title: Secrets
details: Use environment variables, .env files excluded by .gitignore, or a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault).
If a secret reaches Git, assume it is compromised: rotate it, then clean history.

topics.title: Hash vs encrypt vs encode
details: Hashing is one-way (integrity, password storage). Encryption is reversible with a key (confidentiality). Base64 encoding is not security.

topics.title: Using crypto safely
details: Never invent your own crypto; use libraries such as Python's cryptography (Fernet / AES-GCM) and TLS for data in transit.

video.locator: Optional deeper dive: first two lecture segments on what cryptography is and stream ciphers.

reading.locator: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series: 'Secrets Management Cheat Sheet' and 'Password Storage Cheat Sheet'.

assignment.title: Secret hygiene drill
instructions: Add a pre-commit secret scanner (e.g. gitleaks) to your playground repo and show it blocking a fake key.
Store an API key in .env loaded by python-dotenv; confirm .env is ignored.
Encrypt and decrypt a file with cryptography's Fernet; show that tampering is detected.
Write a five-step 'I leaked a key' response plan.
deliverables: Scanner output, code and the response plan.
acceptanceCriteria: The scanner blocks the fake key.
Tampered ciphertext fails to decrypt.

questions.prompt: Is Base64 encryption?
questions.answer: No, it is reversible encoding with no key.
questions.explanation: Anyone can decode it.

questions.prompt: First step after a secret is pushed to GitHub?
questions.answer: Revoke/rotate the secret.
questions.explanation: Deleting the commit is not enough; it may already be copied.

reviewPrompts: Hashing vs encryption?
Where should production secrets live?

modules.title: 14. Communication, interviews and AI-assisted work
modules.description: Skills that decide offers as much as code does: explaining your work, behavioural interviews, a practice routine and using AI tools responsibly.

lessons.title: Explain your work: design docs, demos and project stories
objectives: Write a one-page design doc with context, goals, options, decision and risks.
Explain any project in two minutes: problem, approach, your role, result, what you'd change.
Give a clear five-minute demo.

topics.title: Design docs
details: Context, goals and non-goals, options considered, decision with trade-offs, risks, open questions.

topics.title: Project stories
details: Recruiters ask 'tell me about a project'. Use problem -> constraints -> what you built -> measured result -> lessons.
Use real numbers you measured; never inflate.

topics.title: Speaking
details: Start with the point, use one diagram, show it running, end with limits and next steps.

video.locator: Watch the whole talk; note three techniques you will use.

reading.locator: Technical Writing Essentials: chapter 1 'Introduction to Technical Writing' and the chapter on proposals and reports.

assignment.title: Two project stories
instructions: Write a one-page design doc for one of your MAQ Software workflows (using invented names and no client data) or a personal project.
Record yourself telling two project stories in under two minutes each; listen back and tighten.
deliverables: Design doc and two short written story scripts.
acceptanceCriteria: Stories contain only numbers you can defend.
Each story fits in two minutes.

questions.prompt: What sections does a design doc need?
questions.answer: Context, goals/non-goals, options, decision, risks.
questions.explanation: Options and trade-offs show judgement.

questions.prompt: What makes a project story credible?
questions.answer: Specific, measured results and a clear personal role.
questions.explanation: Vague claims get probed in interviews.

reviewPrompts: Tell your best project story aloud.
What did you learn from recording yourself?

lessons.title: Behavioural interviews, a job-search routine and responsible AI use
objectives: Answer behavioural questions with the STAR structure.
Run a weekly job-search routine: applications, referrals, practice and follow-ups.
Use AI coding assistants to learn faster without outsourcing understanding.

topics.title: STAR
details: Situation, Task, Action (what you did, not the team), Result (measured) and Reflection.
Prepare 6-8 stories: conflict, failure, leadership, tight deadline, learning something fast, disagreement with a decision.

topics.title: Routine
details: Each week: 10-15 targeted applications, 3 referral requests, 5 DSA problems, 1 system-design practice, 1 mock interview.
Track every application in a spreadsheet with status and next action.

topics.title: AI tools
details: Use assistants to explain, generate test ideas and review code; always read, run and understand the result.
In interviews and projects you must be able to explain every line you submit.

reading.locator: Tech Interview Handbook: 'Behavioral interview' section (including the STAR format) and 'Coding interview preparation' study plan.

assignment.title: Story bank and tracker
instructions: Write 6 STAR stories from work or study with real, defensible details.
Set up an application tracker and a weekly calendar block for the routine.
Write your personal rules for using AI assistants while learning.
deliverables: Story bank, tracker screenshot and AI-use rules.
acceptanceCriteria: Each story has a clear personal action and result.
The routine is scheduled in your calendar.

questions.prompt: What does STAR stand for?
questions.answer: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
questions.explanation: Add a short reflection at the end.

questions.prompt: Rule for code an AI assistant wrote for you?
questions.answer: Only use it if you have read, run and understood it.
questions.explanation: You must be able to explain it.

reviewPrompts: Tell a conflict story using STAR.
What is your weekly application target?

sources.title: MIT Missing Semester
sources.notes: Tools every engineer uses but courses rarely teach.

limitations: Skill-builder lessons are beginner-first: each one assumes you have not used the tool before and explains the vocabulary before the practice.
Readings are official documentation or free books, linked rather than copied. Check the current version when you open a link; tools change.
Use your own machine, free tiers and synthetic or public data. Never use employer code, client data or credentials in exercises.
These essentials extend the Common Foundation. They do not replace its eight original modules and are not required to unlock existing projects.
